name: Venezuela
meta_description: Sanctions-screened TDSC consulting on matters touching Venezuela: counterparty due diligence and risk advisory as 2026 OFAC general licences evolve.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting on matters touching Venezuela is governed first by US sanctions, which remain in force but were selectively eased through general licences during 2026. TDSC, a US company, screens every matter and limits its work to lawful due diligence and risk advisory within those rules.
intro: Venezuela has a civil law system, a constitution that recognises habeas data and privacy rights, and an economy dominated for decades by the state oil company PdVSA and other state enterprises. For a US firm the decisive framework is external: the Venezuela Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR Part 591) remain in place, PdVSA has been on the Specially Designated Nationals list since 2019, and dealings with the Government of Venezuela generally require authorisation. From January 2026 OFAC issued a sequence of general licences covering oil and gas trade, services, diluents, telecommunications, coal and aviation safety, each with conditions, while many individuals and entities remain designated.

Organisations commission work touching Venezuela because the 2026 licences have reopened commercial questions that had been dormant. Oil traders, oilfield service companies, shippers, insurers, banks and investors need to know whether a counterparty, vessel or joint venture is owned or controlled by blocked persons, whether proposed terms fit a general licence, and whether parties tied to Russia, Iran, Cuba, North Korea or China are involved. Creditors and litigants pursuing assets, and companies with legacy claims, also require careful background research. Persistent risks include opaque intermediaries, trade-based money laundering, illegal gold mining and reputational exposure to politically connected parties.
legal_system: Venezuela has a civil law system based on codified law, principally the Civil Code and the Code of Commerce, under the 1999 Constitution. The Supreme Tribunal of Justice sits at the apex of the judiciary, and its chambers, including the Constitutional Chamber, issue rulings that have shaped areas such as data protection. Commercial disputes are heard by the ordinary civil and commercial courts. International clients usually prefer arbitration seated outside Venezuela; under some 2026 OFAC general licences, contracts with the Government of Venezuela or PdVSA initially had to be governed by US law with disputes resolved in the United States, a condition OFAC later relaxed and then removed.

data_protection.law: Constitution of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela (1999), Articles 28 (habeas data) and 60 (privacy), as developed by Supreme Tribunal of Justice Decision No. 1318 (2011), with sectoral rules including the Law on Privacy Protection of Communications and the Special Law against Computer Crimes
data_protection.regulator: No national data protection authority; a National Cybersecurity Council created in 2024 has no defined privacy enforcement role
data_protection.summary: Venezuela has no comprehensive data protection statute. Article 28 gives individuals the right to access, rectify and destroy personal data held in public or private records, and Article 60 protects privacy, reputation and confidentiality. Supreme Tribunal Decision No. 1318 of 2011 set out principles including consent, legality, purpose limitation, security and liability, and later decisions protected sensitive medical data and defined personal data. There are no registration, data protection officer or breach notification duties. Recent large breaches, including telecommunications data in 2025, have highlighted the gaps. TDSC applies constitutional principles and the client's own home-jurisdiction rules to any Venezuelan personal data.

investigator_regulation: We have not identified a dedicated licensing regime for private investigators in Venezuela, and we do not rely on that absence. The Law on Privacy Protection of Communications and the Special Law against Computer Crimes restrict interception and unauthorised access to systems, and the political and security climate makes field enquiries sensitive for local participants. For TDSC, the overriding constraint is sanctions: any local step that would involve services to or payments benefiting blocked persons, including Venezuelan government bodies, is excluded unless clearly authorised. Field work is therefore rare and, where considered, is assessed with sanctions counsel and Venezuelan counsel first.
corporate_records: Companies are registered in commercial registries (registros mercantiles) organised by region under the national registries and notaries system. Constitutive documents, by-laws, shareholder assemblies and appointments are recorded in these registries, but there is no reliable public online search, and copies are generally obtained in person through local counsel or agents. We have not identified a public beneficial ownership register. For sanctions purposes, the most authoritative ownership signals often come from OFAC designations and their stated ownership links, corporate filings of foreign parents and joint venture partners, and court and arbitration records abroad.
anti_corruption: Venezuela has a dedicated anti-corruption law and an organised crime and terrorist financing law that includes money laundering offences, enforced by the Public Ministry, the Office of the Comptroller General and the financial intelligence unit; we have not verified the current texts and years for this page. In practice, for clients and investigators outside Venezuela the operative frameworks are their own anti-bribery laws, such as the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, together with US sanctions conditions that prohibit, for example, payment in gold, debt swaps or digital currency under certain 2026 general licences.

matters.title: General licence eligibility reviews
matters.text: Factual research supporting counsel's assessment of whether a proposed oil, gas, services, telecoms or coal transaction fits a 2026 OFAC general licence, including ownership of each party, links to Russia, Iran, Cuba, North Korea or China, and reporting conditions.

matters.title: Counterparty and vessel screening
matters.text: Ownership and control research on traders, shipowners, managers and intermediaries in Venezuelan crude and product flows, testing for blocked persons, 50 percent rule exposure, flag changes and ship-to-ship transfer patterns visible in published maritime data.

matters.title: Joint venture partner background
matters.text: Background research on mixed-company partners, contractors and local service providers for operators and investors re-entering the sector, covering corporate history, designations, litigation abroad and reputational issues, conducted entirely from lawful sources.

matters.title: Creditor and asset research
matters.text: Research on assets and corporate structures connected to Venezuelan obligors located outside Venezuela, for creditors and award holders, carried out within sanctions rules and the protections OFAC and executive orders give to certain blocked or custodial funds.

matters.title: Gold and mining supply chains
matters.text: Screening of refiners, traders and exporters for links to Venezuelan gold, including entities such as Minerven that appear in OFAC licensing, for buyers and banks applying responsible-sourcing and anti-money laundering controls.

tdsc_approach: As a US company, TDSC screens every matter touching Venezuela for sanctions compliance before any work begins, identifying all parties, their owners and their relationship to blocked persons, including the Government of Venezuela and PdVSA. It does not accept engagements that would violate US or other applicable sanctions, and it does not provide services to blocked persons or advise on avoiding sanctions. Most engagements are therefore lawful due diligence and risk advisory for clients outside Venezuela, drawn from OFAC and other official lists, foreign corporate registries, court and arbitration records, maritime data and published reporting. Where a general or specific licence is relevant, TDSC relies on the client's sanctions counsel for the legal conclusion and documents the factual basis supporting it.

faqs.q: Has the United States lifted sanctions on Venezuela?
faqs.a: No. The Venezuela Sanctions Regulations remain in force, PdVSA remains a blocked person and many individuals and entities remain designated. During 2026 OFAC issued general licences authorising specified oil and gas, services, telecommunications, coal and aviation activities under conditions, and adjusted them several times. TDSC treats each licence as narrow and time-sensitive and checks the current text for every matter.

faqs.q: Can TDSC carry out enquiries inside Venezuela?
faqs.a: Rarely. Any local step must be lawful under Venezuelan law and must not involve services to, or payments benefiting, blocked persons, which include Government of Venezuela bodies. Most questions are answered from sources outside the country. Where a local step is proposed, it is reviewed first with sanctions counsel and Venezuelan counsel, and TDSC declines it if the position is unclear.

faqs.q: How do you identify whether a counterparty is owned by a blocked person?
faqs.a: We trace ownership through OFAC designation entries, foreign corporate registries, financing and shipping records, court and arbitration filings and published reporting, then apply the aggregate 50 percent ownership approach as a factual question for counsel. Because Venezuelan commercial registries are not searchable online, conclusions about local entities are stated with their evidential limits.

faqs.q: Does Venezuela have a data protection law?
faqs.a: Not a comprehensive one. Privacy rests on Articles 28 and 60 of the Constitution and on Supreme Tribunal of Justice decisions, notably Decision No. 1318 of 2011, plus sectoral laws on communications privacy and computer crimes. There is no data protection authority. TDSC still applies minimisation and purpose limitation to Venezuelan personal data and follows its clients' own data protection obligations.

faqs.q: Can you help a creditor locate Venezuelan assets?
faqs.a: TDSC can research assets and corporate structures outside Venezuela from lawful sources, provided the engagement is permitted under sanctions rules. Some funds are blocked or held under arrangements, such as those addressed by Executive Order 14373 of January 2026, that limit creditor action. TDSC reports facts; enforcement strategy and licensing questions remain for the client's counsel.
